stem: Best guess: which law governs a contract to sell a used forklift?

choices.text: Common law
choices.explanation: Common law governs services and real estate.

choices.text: UCC Article 9
choices.explanation: Article 9 covers secured transactions.

choices.text: UCC Article 2
choices.explanation: Correct. A forklift is a good.

choices.text: Federal securities law
choices.explanation: A forklift isn't a security.

explanation: Sales of goods (movable tangible property) are governed by UCC Article 2.

stem: A merchant signs a written offer stating it will remain open for 30 days, with no consideration. Can the merchant revoke it after 10 days?

choices.text: Yes, because there's no consideration
choices.explanation: A UCC firm offer needs no consideration.

choices.text: No — all written offers are irrevocable
choices.explanation: Only firm offers or options are.

choices.text: Yes, if the goods cost more than $500
choices.explanation: The price isn't the issue.

choices.text: No — it's a firm offer, irrevocable for the stated period (up to 3 months)
choices.explanation: Correct. UCC 2-205: a merchant's signed written offer that states it will be held open is irrevocable for the stated time, not exceeding 3 months.

explanation: UCC 2-205: a merchant's signed written offer that states it will be held open is irrevocable for the stated time, not exceeding 3 months.

stem: A seller delivers nonconforming goods before the delivery deadline. The buyer rejects them. What right does the seller have?

choices.text: To cure by delivering conforming goods within the contract period
choices.explanation: Correct. UCC 2-508: the seller may cure if the time for performance hasn't expired.

choices.text: None — the buyer's rejection ends the contract
choices.explanation: The seller may cure.

choices.text: To force the buyer to keep the goods at a discount
choices.explanation: The buyer can't be forced to accept.

choices.text: To sue for the full price immediately
choices.explanation: Not while cure is possible.

explanation: UCC 2-508: the seller may cure if the time for performance hasn't expired.

stem: An offeree mails an acceptance on May 1; the offeror mails a revocation on April 30 that arrives May 3. Is there a contract?

choices.text: No — the revocation was sent first
choices.explanation: Revocations are effective on receipt; acceptances on dispatch.

choices.text: No — acceptances are effective only when received
choices.explanation: The mailbox rule makes them effective on dispatch.

choices.text: Yes — the acceptance was effective when dispatched on May 1, before the revocation was received
choices.explanation: Correct. Mailbox rule: acceptance is effective on dispatch (if properly sent); revocation is effective on receipt.

choices.text: Only if the offer was for goods
choices.explanation: The mailbox rule applies generally.

explanation: Mailbox rule: acceptance is effective on dispatch (if properly sent); revocation is effective on receipt.

stem: Which contract must be in writing under the statute of frauds?

choices.text: An oral agreement to paint a house in two weeks for $4,000
choices.explanation: Services performable within a year.

choices.text: A promise to pay one's own debt
choices.explanation: Not a suretyship.

choices.text: An employment contract for six months
choices.explanation: Performable within a year.

choices.text: An agreement to sell goods for $600
choices.explanation: Correct. Goods of $500 or more.

explanation: MY LEGS: goods of $500 or more require a writing.

stem: A contractor promises to finish a job on time but later demands extra pay to finish, which the owner promises. Is the promise enforceable under common law?

choices.text: No — the contractor had a preexisting duty, so there's no new consideration
choices.explanation: Correct. Preexisting duty rule: performing an existing obligation isn't consideration for a new promise (common law).

choices.text: Yes, because the owner agreed
choices.explanation: A preexisting duty isn't consideration.

choices.text: Yes, under the UCC
choices.explanation: Construction is a service, governed by common law.

choices.text: Only if made in writing
choices.explanation: A writing doesn't cure lack of consideration.

explanation: Preexisting duty rule: performing an existing obligation isn't consideration for a new promise (common law).

stem: A 16-year-old buys a gaming laptop and later wants to return it. What is the likely result?

choices.text: The minor is bound
choices.explanation: Minors may disaffirm.

choices.text: The contract is void from the start
choices.explanation: It's voidable, not void.

choices.text: The minor may disaffirm the contract
choices.explanation: Correct. Contracts with minors are voidable at the minor's option (liability for necessaries is limited to reasonable value).

choices.text: Only the seller may cancel
choices.explanation: The minor holds the right to disaffirm.

explanation: Contracts with minors are voidable at the minor's option (liability for necessaries is limited to reasonable value).

stem: Under the parol evidence rule, which evidence may be admitted to vary a fully integrated written contract?

choices.text: An oral agreement made before signing that adds a price discount
choices.explanation: Prior agreements that contradict the writing are barred.

choices.text: Earlier drafts showing different terms
choices.explanation: Prior drafts are barred.

choices.text: A contemporaneous oral agreement changing the delivery date
choices.explanation: Barred for an integrated contract.

choices.text: Evidence that the contract was induced by fraud
choices.explanation: Correct. Exceptions: fraud, duress, mistake, subsequent modifications, and clarifying ambiguity.

explanation: Exceptions: fraud, duress, mistake, subsequent modifications, and clarifying ambiguity.

stem: A contract calls for $50,000 of liquidated damages for late completion; actual losses were hard to estimate and the amount was reasonable. Is it enforceable?

choices.text: No — liquidated damages are never enforced
choices.explanation: They're enforced when reasonable.

choices.text: Yes — it's a reasonable estimate, not a penalty
choices.explanation: Correct. Liquidated damages are enforceable when damages were hard to estimate and the amount is reasonable.

choices.text: Only if actual damages are proven
choices.explanation: Proof of actual damages isn't required.

choices.text: No — punitive damages are required instead
choices.explanation: Punitive damages aren't available for breach.

explanation: Liquidated damages are enforceable when damages were hard to estimate and the amount is reasonable.

stem: A merchant seller ships goods FOB shipping point by common carrier; the goods are destroyed in transit. Who bears the loss?

choices.text: The seller
choices.explanation: Risk passed at delivery to the carrier.

choices.text: The buyer
choices.explanation: Correct. FOB shipping point: risk passes to the buyer when goods are delivered to the carrier.

choices.text: The carrier only
choices.explanation: The carrier may be liable, but between buyer and seller the buyer bears risk.

choices.text: They split it
choices.explanation: The UCC assigns risk to one party.

explanation: FOB shipping point: risk passes to the buyer when goods are delivered to the carrier.

stem: Which statement about the implied warranty of merchantability is correct?

choices.text: It arises in every sale of goods
choices.explanation: Only when the seller is a merchant for those goods.

choices.text: It arises only when the seller is a merchant dealing in goods of that kind
choices.explanation: Correct. UCC 2-314: merchantability is implied only for merchant sellers.

choices.text: It can't be disclaimed
choices.explanation: It can be disclaimed (e.g., "as is" or conspicuous language mentioning merchantability).

choices.text: It requires a written statement
choices.explanation: It's implied by law.

explanation: UCC 2-314: merchantability is implied only for merchant sellers.

stem: A party repudiates a contract before performance is due. What may the other party do?

choices.text: Nothing until the performance date
choices.explanation: It may act immediately.

choices.text: Treat it as a breach and sue immediately, or wait a reasonable time for performance
choices.explanation: Correct. Anticipatory repudiation allows an immediate suit or waiting for performance.

choices.text: Collect punitive damages
choices.explanation: Punitive damages aren't available for breach.

choices.text: Force performance in all cases
choices.explanation: Specific performance is limited.

explanation: Anticipatory repudiation allows an immediate suit or waiting for performance.

stem: Which contract is most likely to be subject to specific performance?

choices.text: A contract to sell a unique parcel of land
choices.explanation: Correct. Specific performance applies when money damages are inadequate — land and unique goods.

choices.text: A contract to sell 100 generic widgets
choices.explanation: Money damages suffice.

choices.text: A personal services contract
choices.explanation: Courts won't compel personal services.

choices.text: A loan agreement
choices.explanation: Money damages suffice.

explanation: Specific performance applies when money damages are inadequate — land and unique goods.
